accuracy.evidence: Each view was checked against solid geometry: a sphere projects to a circle in every direction; a cube to a square from the top and every side; an upright cylinder to a circle (top) and a rectangle (side); an upright cone to a circle with the apex at the centre (top) and an isosceles triangle (side); a square-based pyramid to a square with diagonals meeting at the apex (top) and a triangle (side); a cuboid lying flat to a rectangle (top). Curriculum links quoted from DfE Development Matters 2021 Reception Mathematics and NC 2013 KS1 Geography ('aerial photographs and plan perspectives'). The perspective-taking claims are limited to what Piaget and Inhelder 1956 and Frick, Mohring and Newcombe 2014 report.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets three documented slips: giving the side view for the top view (party hat 'triangle from above' is the step 2 prediction and the 'side' challenge tag), believing the object itself changes when the viewpoint changes (challenge item and the step 2 done message 'the toy did not change; the place you look from did'), and over-generalising that everything looks different from above (step 3 sorts ball and cube as 'same both ways', with its prediction on the ball).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagbirdseye is built on viewpoint itself: toys drawn in three projections (toy, side, top), an eye dragged from beside the toy to a top spot that switches the 'eye sees' panel from side to top view, a same/different sort that compares both projections, a bird-or-child judgement on a single projection, and a bird's-eye plan of a playground. It cannot be relabelled for another topic; the gate measured under 30% shingle overlap with every other flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sees the change happen: moving the eye up turns the hat's triangle into a circle with a dot and the tin's rectangle into a circle, so the idea is discovered before the done line states it. Step 3 then makes them compare both views of five toys, step 4 reverses the question (which place gave this picture), and step 5 applies it to reading a plan.

predictions.evidence: Two predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'a party hat from above looks like a triangle' (step 2 shows a circle with a dot when the eye reaches the top) and 'no, everything changes from above' for the ball (step 3 shows the ball as a circle both ways). The done message reveals the locked-in prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions; every wrong option carries its own tag and message: 'side' (that is the side view; from above you see the top), 'guess' (that shape does not come from this toy), 'tin' and 'hat' (only a ball is a circle from every side), 'change' (the toy stays the same, only the viewpoint changes) and 'plan' (a plan shows things from above, so round is a circle). Step feedback also names the slip, e.g. 'From above, the box is not a circle with a dot'.

readability.evidence: Family lesson for ages 4 to 5: kid text is FK grade 0.8 in short sentences of common words ('A bird flies high up. It looks down.'); adult text is FK 6.3, within the 10.0 limit. Canvas text is one short line per card at 13 to 16 px, and every step can be done with a grown-up reading the banner aloud.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passes (no filler phrases; under 12% overlap with any other lesson). Kid paragraphs each teach one point (what a bird's-eye view is, the hat, the tin and ball, plans); adult paragraphs give the curriculum link, the views of six solids, the perspective-taking research with a home tip, and the named mistakes with a lab summary.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 (light and dark) and 360 x 640 Android (dark) screenshots of all six steps: the four top-view bins fit in one row with their labels shrunk to fit ('Circle with a dot' on two lines), the eye stays fully on screen with a dotted sight line to the toy, the sort boxes and bird/child buttons are half-width, the plan fills the canvas, and the young class gives large buttons under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button: four top-view buttons naming the toy, Look from the side and Look from above naming the toy, Same both ways and Different naming the toy, Bird from above and Child at the side, and one button per plan item. note() updates the canvas aria-label and the polite live region after every action; the walk gate's axe run (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
